TERYLENE SAILS because: Though more expensive, they are smoother and give higher performance than cotton. They are strong, and keep their strength when wet. No stretchin g out of shape, unless a light sail is pressed hard in heavy weather. They can thus be cut nearer to their marks, giving more sail area. They absorb less moisture so less weight is carried aloft. When wet, they remain light, flexible and easy to handle. They dry quickly and take up less room when stowed. But they sometimes mildew if put away wet. However they are not weakened by mildew, bacteria or sunlight. TERYLENE CORDAGE becauses Stronger than manilla or hemp, it keeps strength when wet. It takes a load without excessive stretching,an advantage for sheets. It does not shrink when wet, an advantage for halyards, lanyards and outhauls. Wet or dry, it is easy to handle. Its high coefficient of friction gives it a good grip on winch barrels, It is not rotted by sunlight, mildew or sea slime. HOW DO I STRETCH NEW TERYLENE SAILS? The same general principles apply as for cotton Sails. Set new Tepylene sails with care, so that the seams settle down evenly. ~ Pull the foot of your sail well out until the wrinkles disappear and do not sheet it in for the first hour or so. Haul up on your halyard and out on your clew outhaul an inch or so at a time, to keep pace with the stretching of the luff rope and the foot rope. Two or three hours sailing in a gentle breeze should get the sail near its marks. Make sure that your gooseneck fitting is not too high. The tack cringle must be in line with the foot of the sail. Let us briefly review a few of the requirements of the cruiser, Firstly, it must be self-sufficient, carrying tools and materials for running repairs and either buoyancy materials or a dinghy capable of saving the crew in an extreme emergency. It should not be necessxry to mention that the hull must be basically SEAworthy - not just DITCHworthy and strong enough to take the inevitable knock in harbour. A boat which can be holed by a day tripper in a roaming boat can hardly be strong enough for the rough and tumble of cruising. Secondly, a cruiser must have space to sleep the crew — 6'6" x 2' per person. On an ocean race, there may be more crew than bunks, but then, there will always be at least one man on watch, The next essential is adequate space and facilities for preparing and easing HOT nourishing meals. When cruising, a tin of self-heating soup and a packet of biscuits does NOT constitute a meal. At least one stove should be capable of use whilst sailing in the worst of conditions as this is when a hot meal is most likely to be needed. Next, a cruiser should have ample stowage space for food, water, spare clothing, charts, tools, ropes and all the spare sailing gear. A fixed cabin (or even a deck!) does not automatically make a boat suitable for cruising = in fact, one of the best equipped small cruisers sailing ~ from Maldon is a 13' three quarter decked dinghy, a beamy seawaorthy hull witha snug gunter rig, a small inboard engine, and numerous lockers, clips and shelves for the gear and a canvas cover to sleep under. B) CRUISING IN A RACING DINGHY by "Barnacle" In experiences hands, the smallest of racing dinghies can be used for cruising, provided the owner is prepared to put up with certain inconven- iences, chief of which is the need to put ashore to sleep and often to eat a good meal. To be satisfactory as a cruiser, the boat must have ample buoyancy and sufficient space in which to lash all the gear securely. Cruising in a racing dinghy differs from normal cruising in that the cruise must be planned on a day-to-day basis and a careful watch kept on the weather. Also, more precautions must be taken. It is as well to keep the gear carried at a minimum and to stow as much as possible in the centre of the boat, round the plate case, using the toe straps to tie it in. It is also well to plan the cruise so that nights can be spent at Youth Hostels, boarding houses or hotels, according to the depth of one's pockets, but arrange for alternative ports of call in case wind or tide misbehave, and do not try to do too much in any one day = a long beat in a rough sea is very wearying and if you do capsize (T.W.H. to note!) you may be too tired to right the boat. It is often good policy to use an undersize suit of sails ~ the Enterprise has a Special cruising rig which is smaller than the usual racing rig - and do not be afraid to reef - you won't lose any points if you take another hour to get there, but you may lose your life or your boat, if you are not careful. Unless the weather is exceptionally settled, it is wise to wear personal buoyancy all the time and tie the end of a sheet around your waist( after making sure that it will not pull away from the sail or boom). Compass, charts, tide tables, waterproof torches, a good anchor and warps must be added to the boat's normal gear, and it is a good idea to carry a couple of large Thermos flasks in clips in the aft end of the cockpit. A trapeze and a good self-bailer will make life easier for the crusijg dinghy owner. A boat with a large open cockpit can be improved by fitting canvas aprons over as much of it as practicable. Personal gear can be limited to a complete change of clothing and toilet kit, but take a good suit of oilskins. If you are a smoker, be sure your cigarettes are well wrapped up and carry lots of boxes of matches. 5 SOME POINTS TO CONSIDER ON BUYING A SMALL CRUISER by "Barnacle" Maybe some of you are planning to visit the Boat Show with a view to buying a small cruiser. Be careful what you buy. You are going to spend something oyer £200. Be sure you get value for your money and get a boat in which you can cruise in comfort without partially re-building it or, if you have any skill with tools, and any spare time, get a hull, spars and sails and do the cabin interior yourself, Some firms produce small cruisers with a superb finish - varnished all over. Avoid these like the plague. A varnished interior is useless on a small cruiser aS it will make the cabin look smaller than it is and whatever boat you buy, you will find you would like a larger cabin. Also, once the initial high gloss has gone from the varnish, you will find the cabin will be a miserable gloomy place in which to live, even for one night. A pastel shade of enamel is a far better finish as it will make the cabin look much bigger, warmer and lighter. White is not good as it is cold and soon gets grubby, showing all the dirt. Blue also tends to be cold but is reputed not to attract flies and other insects. If vou want to see the grain and colour of any timber inside the boat, use a Wax polish and you can touch it up any time and not have to leave it for a day to dry. Whilst on the subject of apparent size, get a boat with the minimum of bulkheads. A bridge deck between cabin and cockpit is good for keeping the cabin dry but the only other bulkhead needed is a small one near the bowe Any other bulkheads will divide the precious cabin space into smaller units and will make the accommodation look more cramped than it really ise You need onlt glance at two otherwise identical hulls, one with a bulkhead or partial bulkhead by the mast, and one with the bulkhead about 3 ft. from the stem, to realise the vast difference in the apparent amount of room in the hull. Curtains can be used when required for screening off pamt of the hull. Be sure adequate provision has been made for carrying fresh water, for cooking and for toilet facilities. One gimballed cre, (aR a Primus) just inside the aft end of the cabin with a shelf near on which a saucepan and kettle can be stood is the minimum to be asked of a small cruiser. Be sure the stove is not mounted too high and that it has s sheet of asbestos above it, for otherwise your cabin top will soon be filthy. A plastic bucket under a’ small plywood locker is the best form of toilet for a miniature cruiser. Bunks should be at least 6'6" long and 22" wide, though they may taper to as kow as 10" at the foot. Be sure that some arrangement has heen made to prevent you slipping off the bunk when the boat rolls. Incidentally, 3' head- room is adequate for sitting in comfort. Obviously, you will not be able to stand up in a small cruiser and since 3' is more than adequate for crawling about there is really no need for an excessively high cabin top. Get a boat with the floorbo,rds raised high enough to stow tinned food and the inevitable bilge water underneath; it is most unpleasant to put your . foot in cold water on getting out of your nice warm sleeping bage Ample storage space is a necessity in a cruiser but remember that one vast locker or innumerable small lockers are both bad - three or four medium sized lockers will enable you to keep food seperate from clothing etc. and will alse be fairly easy to keep clean. Small shelves between the frames of the boat with 3" perspex fronts are handy for stowing odds and ends but be sure the corners of the shelves are cut away so they will not trap water. Some form of table is also highly desirable. It may be hinged to the side of the boat over one of the buhks or it may be stowed out of the way by clipping up under the deck. Adequate ventilation of the cabin is another essential and be sure the ventilators are fitted with water traps. Some form of extractor vent over the stove is another good feature. Avoid large cabin windows for they easily get covered in spray and dirt and weaken the cabin sides unduly. SOME POINTS TO CONSIDER ON BUYING A SMALL CRUISER by "Barnacle" Sa I have already aired the various snags and merits of centreboards, leeboards, bilge keels and fixed keels in this series of srticles, so the only point I will make here is - go for simplicity if you buy a centreboarder. Avoid dagger plate types - they are alright on a racing dinghy but tend to need excessively elaborate gear on a cruiser and they project too high into the cabin if they are even reasonable size —- remember it is depth of plate that counts, not just area. The question of Bermudian or Gaff rig is too big to be considered in this article but one point I must make here is —- get a sloop rig. If you go cutter, your headsails will probably be too small to be of much real use and the onl% real reason for multi-mast and multi-sail rigs is to keep individual sails down to a size that can be easily handled. If the mast is stepped on deck, make sure the deck is well strenghhened to take it, preferably with a post down to the keel. While examining the rigging, make sure the boat has adequate chain plates well secured to the hull and if the rigging screws are used, see they are so fitted that no bending strain can be put on the threadse Check up on the metals used in the rigging assembly and indeed in the whole boat and be certain there are no likely sources of electrol- ytic action. Iron bilge keels riveted to the hull with copper rivets, iron straps with brass rivets and rigging screws with male and female members of: —_ different metals are three common examples. —- If the boat you contemplate buying has a fairly high cabin top, be sure the side decks are wide enough to enable you to reach the foredeck easily and quickly, going inside the shrouds. If the boat has a lower full width cabin top, check that it is easy of access from the cockpit. Whatever type of cabin top the boat has, be sure it has a good handrail which can be easily grasped, even if your hand is half wrapped up in a spare handsail and also a toe rail one or two inches high all round the edge of the deck with adequate holes in it to let the water drain off the deck. On the foredeck, see the boat has adequate provision for securing the warps, either a stout ringbolt, cleat or post well secured to the framework of the hull, and good fairheads through which to lead the warps. Chocks should be provided in which to secure the anchor whilst sailing and there should be stowage space handy for the warp, unless the boat is fitted with a navel pipe and the warp stowed below. If the main cabib entrance has a sliding hatch, make sure it slidus easily and is of a type which will keep leaks to a minimum. If hinged cabin doors are fitted they should be on a "lift off" type hinge with a larger pin on the bottor hinge than the top. ee Lastle the finish of the boat. Varnish looks nice when it is new but it is a swine to keep looking good. It is better to have the hull enamelled and only the cabin sides and the trimmings and of course, the spars, varnished. A varnished deck is hopeless. As soon as it gets wet it will be dangerously slippery and anyway the varnish will not last long. The deck surface should be rough, but not so rough that you would hurt yourself if you fell. The owner of a racing dinghy during the Winter and on non-sailing days in the Summer will create the right impression if he appears in a freshly laundered white overall, of a non-fluffy material, with an outsize tin of Blanks silicone polish in one pocket, a good pile of polishing cloths and, at painting time, a wet and dry bulb hygrometer. One or teo carefully positioned paint splashes on the overall are admissible but should not be overdone. Whilst the other Club members are happily slapping on paint, the expert will measure the humid- ity and estimate the dust content of the atmosphere and decide that conditions hardly favour the perfect finish, so will spend the day working on the Beel band with "Brasso", then, when no-one is about, he can comfortably remove his immaculate overalls, don a couple of fluffy old sweaters and slosh on some paint. This way he will get the same quality finish overall as all the rest, but he will have created a far better impression.
